A performance rule only means something while the machine is running. A PV panel producing 0 kW at night is normal, and alarming on it teaches users to ignore alarms.
The default is INSPECT, not repair: the alarm says there is a sign of something wrong, not what is broken. Opening a repair order straight away is concluding before looking.
Counts how many times an alarm COMES BACK after a repair order was closed. Above 0 means the previous repair did not hold — this is the only way to tell "repaired" from "order closed".
One sentence for the whole batch, but each alarm still records\n who acknowledged it and when — three months later each one\n can still be traced.

A band uses both Threshold (lower) and Upper threshold. "Outside the band" is what is needed most often: gearbox temperature too high OR too low both matter, and two separate rules mean fixing things twice.
Only for SENSOR-DEVIATION rules: two sensors measuring the same quantity that disagree beyond the threshold mean one of them has drifted — and looking at one alone tells you nothing about which.

Addressed by CODE, not by record: one rule has to work across every plant that follows the same code convention. End with "*" to match several points — "T*_TGB" is gearbox temperature on every turbine.
%(ten)s has not sent a reading for %(gio).1f hours (last at %(c)s). While it is silent, every threshold rule watching this same tag is silent too — check the LINK before sending anyone up the tower.
Thresholds belong on CONDITION meters (vibration, oil temperature). Putting one on running hours duplicates the preventive maintenance plan, and then two mechanisms raise orders for the same job.
No readings means the link is dead, not the\n machine. The thing to do is check the\n connection — do not send anyone up the tower.
Two sensors disagree by %(l).1f%%: %(a)s is at %(va).3f, %(b)s is at %(vb).3f. One of them has drifted — and taken separately both sit in a plausible range, so only this comparison reveals it.

Close it against the order so that the indicator "what share of failures was caught before energy was lost" has data. Leave it open and that column stays empty for good, and condition monitoring cannot prove it pays for itself.
Putting a threshold on running hours duplicates\n the preventive maintenance plan — and then two\n mechanisms raise orders for the same job.

Alarms arrive from rules scanning meters, from outside systems pushing them in, or from an operator reporting one. Each row is an episode — being raised again within the episode only adds to the count, it does not create a new row.
This is the list of repairs that did not hold: alarms that\n were closed by a work order and then came back. It is the only way to\n tell "repaired" from "order closed".

The moment the system FIRST RECORDED the condition — not the moment an operator opened the screen to look, and not the moment the alarm was raised again later: a later occurrence adds to "times raised" and updates "last seen", while this stamp stays put.

A snooze always has a deadline. At the deadline the system reopens it and writes a note on the alarm — silencing something for good is how a plant loses a whole layer of watchfulness with nobody remembering what was turned off.
Meter stalled means readings keep arriving while the running hours do not increase: the machine really is down. Quite different from no readings — confusing the two sends you the wrong way.
The rule decides what counts as abnormal and what to do when it fires.\n The alarm log is source-agnostic: today it runs on meters and\n operators; when SCADA arrives it is simply one more source.

The condition has to hold for this many minutes before an alarm is raised. Set 0 to raise it at once.\n\nThis is what separates a usable set of alarms from one that gets switched off in the first week: a single noisy sample also crosses the threshold, and people put up with about a dozen false alarms before ignoring the lot.
Create at once should be reserved for critical severity. One noisy sensor raising 500 alarms in a night becomes 500 junk orders, after which nobody reads the order list any more — real ones included.

Create order now should be reserved for critical severity. One noisy sensor raising 500 alarms in a night becomes 500 junk orders, after which nobody reads the order list any more.\n\n"Open a REQUEST" is the right choice for low-level alarms: it goes into the request log for the dispatcher to judge whether an order is warranted, instead of straight onto the list of work to be done.
